name: Calcutta
historicalStatus: Imperial Capital of British India & Lieutenant-Governorship of Bengal
descriptionShort: Calcutta was the imperial capital of British India and the Lieutenant-Governorship of Bengal. Famous for Esplanade, Fort William, High Court, Bengal Renaissance, and Swadeshi protests.
descriptionLong:
Founded in 1690 by Job Charnock through the unification of three villages (Kalikata, Sutanuti, and Gobindapur), Calcutta developed into the 'City of Palaces' and the supreme administrative, commercial, and judicial heart of British India. By 1905, it was the second largest city in the British Empire after London, boasting premier institutions like Calcutta University, the High Court, Fort William, and Indian Museum.

Famed for its intellectual Bengal Renaissance, publishing houses, College Street book market, and international jute trade along the Hugli river, Calcutta was the central nerve center of anti-partition politics in 1905.
famousSpecialties: Bengal Renaissance literature & printing, College Street publishing, Jute mills along Hugli river, Fort William, Esplanade, and premier educational universities.
revolutionarySignificance: Nerve center of the 1905 Swadeshi Movement. Site of Rabindranath Tagore's Rakhi Bandhan march, Anushilan Samiti headquarters, and Barindra Kumar Ghosh's secret Maniktala bomb laboratory (Alipore Bomb Case, 1908).

politicalHistory.ruler: Sena successor chiefs, Delhi governors & Bengal Sultanate
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The settlement lay in the lower delta, successively within Sena remnants, the Delhi Sultanate's Bengal provinces, and the independent Bengal Sultanate.

politicalHistory.ruler: Mughal Empire, then the Nawabs of Bengal
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Mughal Bengal absorbed the lower Hugli region after 1576; the Nawabs exercised effective provincial authority from Murshidabad after 1717.

politicalHistory.ruler: East India Company zamindari at Calcutta
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The Company acquired zamindari rights in Calcutta, Sutanuti and Govindapur in 1698, while the Nawab remained sovereign over the surrounding province.

politicalHistory.ruler: East India Company under a nominal Nawab
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The Company installed Mir Jafar after Plassey and became the decisive power around Fort William, though Mughal-Nawabi forms remained visible.

politicalHistory.ruler: East India Company (Diwani and Presidency government)
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The 1765 Diwani grant gave the Company Bengal's revenue; direct administration followed in 1772 and Calcutta became the imperial governing centre.
After the 1857 transfer of power, Calcutta remained the Viceroy's capital and the seat of Bengal's government.

politicalHistory.ruler: British Crown: Bengal divided; Calcutta in Western Bengal
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The partition placed Calcutta in the reduced Bengal province; the city remained the centre of anti-partition politics.
Bengal was reunited in 1912, but the imperial capital moved to Delhi; Calcutta remained Bengal's capital and premier port.
Partition placed Calcutta in India as the capital of West Bengal; it continues as Kolkata, the state's constitutional and cultural capital.

name: Dacca
historicalStatus: Division Headquarters & Capital of Eastern Bengal & Assam (Oct 1905)
descriptionShort: Dacca was the historical capital of Mughal Subah Bangalah (as Jahangirnagar) and world-renowned center of fine Jamdani muslin weaving.
descriptionLong:
Established as the Mughal capital of Bengal by Subahdar Islam Khan I in 1610, Dacca grew into a wealthy riverine metropolis famed for its architectural monuments (Lalbagh Fort, Ahsan Manzil, Bara Katra) and unmatched Dhaka Muslin craftsmanship exported across the globe.

On 16 October 1905, Dacca was named the capital of the newly created province of Eastern Bengal and Assam under Lieutenant-Governor Sir Joseph Bampfylde Fuller. In November 1905, Pulin Behari Das founded the Dhaka Anushilan Samiti here, establishing a network of over 500 revolutionary secret branches. In December 1906, Ahsan Manzil hosted the founding conference of the All-India Muslim League.
famousSpecialties: World-famous Dhaka Jamdani Muslin textiles, Nawabi Mughlai cuisine, riverine jute trade, Lalbagh Fort architecture, and shell-carving (Shankhari) craft.
revolutionarySignificance: Birthplace of Dhaka Anushilan Samiti founded by Pulin Behari Das in Nov 1905, establishing over 500 underground revolutionary branches across East Bengal delta districts.

politicalHistory.ruler: Sena successor rulers, Deva dynasty and Bengal Sultanate
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Dacca lay within the changing political landscape of eastern Bengal, near the Deva and later Sultanate centres of Vikramapura and Sonargaon; it was not yet the provincial capital.

politicalHistory.ruler: Mughal Empire contested by the Baro-Bhuyans
politicalHistory.periodDetails: After the Mughal conquest of Bengal, the Bhati region remained contested. Isa Khan and other river chiefs exercised substantial authority around Dacca before Mughal consolidation.
Subahdar Islam Khan defeated the Bhati chiefs and transferred the provincial capital from Rajmahal to Dacca in 1610, renaming it Jahangirnagar.

politicalHistory.ruler: Mughal Empire under the Bengal subahdars
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The provincial administration gradually shifted from Dacca toward Murshidabad as Murshid Quli Khan consolidated the diwani and revenue machinery.

politicalHistory.ruler: Nawabs of Bengal under nominal Mughal sovereignty
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Murshidabad became the de facto capital, while Dacca remained the leading city and administrative centre of eastern Bengal, renowned for muslin production.

politicalHistory.ruler: Nawabs of Bengal under East India Company influence
politicalHistory.periodDetails: After Plassey, the Company became the decisive power in Bengal, while Dacca continued under the Nawab's provincial administration.
The Company's Diwani of 1765 brought Dacca district into its revenue system; the city remained an important commercial and administrative centre.
Dacca was administered as the headquarters of Dacca Division under Crown rule, with municipal institutions and expanding colonial infrastructure.

politicalHistory.ruler: British Crown: Eastern Bengal and Assam
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The first partition made Dacca the capital of the new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam under Lieutenant-Governor Sir Bampfylde Fuller.
The partition was annulled and Dacca reverted to a divisional and district headquarters within reunited Bengal, while Calcutta remained the provincial capital.
Partition placed Dacca in Pakistan's eastern wing; it became the provincial capital of East Bengal and the principal political centre of the region.
After the province was renamed East Pakistan in 1955, Dacca remained its capital and the centre of the language, autonomy and independence movements.
Dacca became the capital of independent Bangladesh after the Liberation War and is now known as Dhaka, the country's national capital.

name: Murshidabad
historicalStatus: Capital of the Nawabs of Bengal (1717–1757)
descriptionShort: Murshidabad was the grand capital of the Nawabs of Bengal on the Bhagirathi river, famous for Hazarduari Palace, fine Baluchari silk weaving, and Jagat Seth banking house.
descriptionLong:
Founded when Nawab Murshid Quli Khan transferred the revenue court from Dacca in 1717, Murshidabad became one of the wealthiest commercial centers in Asia. It witnessed the momentous events surrounding Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah, the Battle of Plassey, Hazarduari Palace, Katra Mosque, and Khosbagh tombs.

Famed for its traditional Baluchari silk weaving and ivory carving, Murshidabad was also an active station during the 1857 Sepoy Mutiny (Berhampore Cantonment) and produced prominent revolutionary organizers during the Swadeshi movement.
famousSpecialties: Baluchari silk sarees, Ivory carving heritage, Murshidabad Shahi sweets (Chanabora), Hazarduari Palace museum, and Katra Mosque architecture.
revolutionarySignificance: Site of the first spark of the 1857 Sepoy Revolt at Berhampore Cantonment (19th Native Infantry) and active Swadeshi boycott meetings along the Bhagirathi river.

politicalHistory.periodDetails: The Bhagirathi basin moved from the early Lakhnauti governors into the independent Bengal Sultanate; the Murshidabad area was within its western and central provinces.
After Rajmahal, Mughal officers governed the region through sarkars and parganas; local zamindars continued to mediate revenue and landholding.

politicalHistory.ruler: Mughal Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Murshid Quli Khan shifted the diwani administration from Dacca to the Murshidabad area, laying the foundation for its capital status.
Murshidabad was the de facto capital of the wealthy Bengal Subah under Murshid Quli Khan, Shuja-ud-Din, Alivardi Khan and Siraj-ud-Daulah.

politicalHistory.ruler: Nawabs under East India Company influence
politicalHistory.periodDetails: After Plassey, the Company controlled succession and finance while the Nawab's court remained at Murshidabad.
The Company acquired the Diwani in 1765 and assumed direct civil administration in 1772; Murshidabad's political role became largely ceremonial.
The Nawab Bahadur survived as a titular estate holder under British paramountcy while Berhampore served as the principal district and cantonment centre.
Partition placed Murshidabad in India; the former capital is now a historic town within the Republic of India's West Bengal state.

name: Chittagong
historicalStatus: Major Deepwater Port & Division Headquarters
descriptionShort: Chittagong was Bengal's principal eastern deepwater seaport on the Karnaphuli river, known historically as Porto Grande to Portuguese traders.
descriptionLong: A major maritime port since antiquity, Chittagong linked Bengal to Arakan, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East. Captured by Mughal Prince Shaista Khan in 1666 and renamed Islamabad, it passed to the East India Company in 1760. In 1905, it served as the chief ocean outlet for tea and jute from Eastern Bengal and Assam, later becoming famous for Surya Sen's 1930 Chittagong Armoury Raid.
famousSpecialties: Deepwater maritime shipping, Assam-Bengal Railway terminus, tea export warehouse, and traditional wooden shipbuilding along the Karnaphuli river.
revolutionarySignificance: Strategic maritime hub for revolutionary secret arms shipments; later site of Surya Sen's (Masterda) legendary 1930 Chittagong Armoury Raid and Jalalabad Hill battle.

politicalHistory.ruler: Local Harikela and eastern Bengal chiefs
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The port lay in the politically distinct southeast, where local dynasties and coastal chiefs retained authority beyond the reach of the early Lakhnauti governors.
Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah of Sonargaon conquered Chittagong in 1340; later Ilyas Shahi and Husain Shahi sultans governed the port through appointed officials.

politicalHistory.ruler: Kingdom of Arakan (Mrauk U) and Portuguese commanders
politicalHistory.periodDetails: As Bengal's sultanate weakened, Arakanese power and Portuguese mercenaries or privateers dominated the port and its maritime approaches.
Shaista Khan's forces expelled Arakanese and Portuguese power in 1666, incorporated the port into Bengal Subah and renamed it Islamabad.
Nawab Mir Qasim ceded Chittagong to the Company in 1760; it became a British district headquarters and an expanding port.
Chittagong remained under Crown administration, with municipal government from 1863 and port administration increasingly formalized.

politicalHistory.ruler: British Crown: Eastern Bengal and Assam
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The partition transferred Chittagong Division to the new eastern province, making the port a major outlet for Assam and eastern Bengal.
Chittagong returned to the reconstituted Bengal administrative system while retaining its strategic port and divisional role.

politicalHistory.ruler: Pakistan: East Bengal, later East Pakistan
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Partition placed Chittagong in Pakistan's eastern wing; the port became its principal maritime gateway.
Liberation in 1971 placed Chittagong in Bangladesh; it is now Chattogram, the country's major port city.

name: Patna
historicalStatus: Headquarters of Patna Division & Capital of Bihar
descriptionShort: Patna was the historic capital of Bihar on the Ganges, ancient Pataliputra, famous for the Golghar granary and agricultural opium and grain trade.
descriptionLong: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, ancient Pataliputra was capital of the Mauryan and Gupta empires under Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka. Rebuilt by Sher Shah Suri in 1541 and renamed Azimabad under Prince Azim-ush-Shan, Patna served as headquarters of Patna Division in 1905, handling river trade for opium, saltpetre, and indigo along the Ganges.
famousSpecialties: Ancient Pataliputra archaeological heritage, historic Golghar granary, Ganges riverine trade, and traditional Madhubani & Patna Qalam painting styles.
revolutionarySignificance: Key center during the 1857 Revolt led by Kunwar Singh of Jagdishpur; later active in Swadeshi revolutionary cells across Bihar.

politicalHistory.periodDetails: Patna and the Ganges corridor were governed through successive Delhi Sultanate governors and local landed authorities.

politicalHistory.ruler: Mughal Empire under Babur and Humayun
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Mughal authority extended into Bihar but remained contested by Afghan nobles.

politicalHistory.ruler: Sur Empire (Sher Shah Suri and successors)
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Sher Shah rebuilt the city and its roads as a strategic centre of his Bihar-based empire.

politicalHistory.ruler: Mughal Empire, then the Nawabs of Bengal
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Patna became the headquarters of Bihar under Mughal subahdars and later a key city of the Bengal Nawabs.
The Diwani grant and the Company's victory at Buxar brought Patna into the Bengal Presidency's revenue and judicial system.
Patna remained the headquarters of Patna Division under Crown rule.

politicalHistory.ruler: British Crown: Bihar and Orissa Province
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The 1912 reorganization separated Bihar and Orissa from Bengal and made Patna the provincial capital.
Orissa became a separate province in 1936; Patna continued as Bihar's capital until independence.
Patna became the capital of the Indian state of Bihar after independence and remains so today.

name: Cuttack
historicalStatus: Headquarters of Orissa Division & Ancient Capital of Odisha
descriptionShort: Cuttack was the traditional riverine delta capital of Orissa at the Mahanadi river apex, famous for Barabati Fort, silver filigree craft, and Utkal Sammilani movement.
descriptionLong: Founded in the 10th century CE by King Nrupa Keshari, Cuttack served as the political capital of successive Eastern Ganga and Gajapati dynasties. Captured by the British in 1803 during the Second Anglo-Maratha War, it became the administrative headquarters of the Orissa Division within the Bengal Presidency. Famous for exquisite Tarakasi (silver filigree) jewelry.
famousSpecialties: Tarakasi (Silver Filigree) jewelry, Barabati Fort heritage, Katasa handloom sarees, and birthplace of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose (1897).
revolutionarySignificance: Birthplace of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose (23 Jan 1897); headquarters of Madhusudan Das's Utkal Sammilani movement advocating Oriya administrative rights.

politicalHistory.ruler: Eastern Ganga and Gajapati kings of Odisha
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Cuttack was the fortified capital of the Ganga and Gajapati kingdoms, which controlled coastal Odisha and resisted Bengal-based powers.

politicalHistory.ruler: Bengal Sultanate, Mughal Empire and local zamindars
politicalHistory.periodDetails: After the fall of Mukunda Deva, Bengal's Karrani rulers and then Mughal subahdars governed Cuttack through the Orissa administration.
The Marathas held Orissa after the Nawab of Bengal ceded it during the settlement following the Bargi raids.
The Company occupied Cuttack in 1803 during the Second Anglo-Maratha War and made it the administrative headquarters.
Cuttack continued as the headquarters of Orissa Division under Crown administration.

politicalHistory.ruler: British Crown: Bihar and Orissa Province
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Orissa was separated administratively from Bengal in 1912, with Cuttack retaining its divisional importance.
Orissa became a separate province in 1936; Cuttack served as its capital and principal administrative city.
Cuttack joined India in 1947 and remained Odisha's capital until Bhubaneswar became the political capital in 1948; it remains the state's historic commercial centre.

name: Ranchi
historicalStatus: Headquarters of Chota Nagpur Division
descriptionShort: Ranchi was the plateau headquarters of Chota Nagpur Division, home to Munda and Oraon tribal communities and center of Birsa Munda's Ulgulan uprising.
descriptionLong: Selected as the headquarters of the South-West Frontier Agency in 1834 and later Chota Nagpur Division, Ranchi developed into a cool summer station on the Chota Nagpur plateau. It was the epicenter of Birsa Munda's famous Ulgulan (rebellion) of 1899–1900 against British land encroachment and forced labor.
famousSpecialties: Plateau climate, Hundru & Dassam waterfalls, tribal handicrafts, lac production, and sacred Munda Sarna traditions.
revolutionarySignificance: Epicenter of Birsa Munda's historic Ulgulan (Great Tumult) uprising (1899–1900) against British land encroachment and zamindari exploitation.

politicalHistory.ruler: Nagvanshi kings and local Munda-Oraon chiefs
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The plateau was governed by the Nagvanshi polity and village chiefs, with changing claims of tribute from Bengal, Bihar and the Mughals.

politicalHistory.ruler: East India Company and Nagvanshi estate
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Company revenue authority expanded after the Diwani, while the Nagvanshi ruler and customary tribal institutions retained local influence.
Ranchi became the headquarters of the frontier agency as Company officials reorganized the plateau's revenue and policing.
Ranchi served as divisional and district headquarters; the 1899–1900 Ulgulan exposed the limits of colonial land policy.
Chota Nagpur remained with the western province rather than joining Eastern Bengal and Assam.

politicalHistory.ruler: British Crown: Bihar and Orissa Province
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The 1912 reorganization placed Ranchi in Bihar and Orissa, with the plateau administered through the Chota Nagpur Division.
After Orissa separated, Ranchi remained a major Bihar divisional headquarters.
Ranchi became part of independent India and continued as a major administrative centre of Bihar.
Ranchi became the capital of the newly created state of Jharkhand on 15 November 2000.

name: Darjeeling
historicalStatus: Summer Capital of Bengal Lieutenant-Governorship
descriptionShort: Darjeeling was the Himalayan hill station and official summer seat of the Bengal Government, famed for world-renowned Darjeeling Tea and Kangchenjunga views.
descriptionLong: Acquired by the East India Company from the Chogyal of Sikkim in 1835 as a sanatorium, Darjeeling was transformed by Dr. Arthur Campbell into a premier hill station and tea hub. In 1881, the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway (Toy Train) reached the town, making it accessible as Bengal's official summer capital.
famousSpecialties: World-famous Darjeeling Orthodox Tea plantations, Darjeeling Himalayan Railway (Toy Train, UNESCO), Kangchenjunga panoramas, and Himalayan botanical gardens.
revolutionarySignificance: Official summer administrative seat of the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal; later site of revolutionary assassination attempt on Governor Sir John Anderson (1934).

politicalHistory.ruler: Sikkimese, Gorkha and local Himalayan authorities
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The hill tract was outside the settled Bengal plains and was governed through shifting Sikkimese and Gorkha claims.
Gorkha expansion brought much of the Darjeeling hills under Nepalese control before the Anglo-Nepalese War.

politicalHistory.ruler: British East India Company and Kingdom of Sikkim
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The Treaty of Titalia established British influence; the Darjeeling tract was transferred to the Company in 1835.
The Company developed Darjeeling as a sanatorium and hill station while recognizing Sikkim's residual frontier claims.
Darjeeling became the Lieutenant-Governor's summer seat and a district under Crown administration.
Darjeeling remained with the western Bengal province while eastern Bengal and Assam was created.
Darjeeling continued as Bengal's summer administrative centre until the end of British rule.
Darjeeling joined India as part of West Bengal; the hills remain within the state with changing autonomous arrangements.

name: Burdwan
historicalStatus: Burdwan Division Headquarters & Seat of Raj Bardhaman
descriptionShort: Burdwan was the headquarters of Burdwan Division and home to the Maharajadhiraja of Burdwan, premier zamindari estate of Bengal, famous for Curzon Gate.
descriptionLong: Situated on the Banka river, Burdwan was an ancient seat of culture and commerce. The Maharaja of Burdwan was the highest tax-paying zamindar in British India. In 1903, the grand Curzon Gate was erected to welcome Viceroy Lord Curzon. The district featured the 108 Shiva Temples of Kalna and major coalfields in Raniganj and Asansol.
famousSpecialties: Sitabhog & Mihidana sweet delicacies, Curzon Gate landmark, 108 Shiva Temples of Kalna, and Raniganj coalfields.
revolutionarySignificance: Active center during the Swadeshi boycott; produced prominent freedom fighters and underground press distributors across West Bengal.

politicalHistory.ruler: Sena successor chiefs and Bengal Sultanate
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The Damodar-Ajay tract passed from post-Sena local rulers into the western provinces of the Bengal Sultanate.
Mughal authority was exercised through revenue officers and local zamindars after the conquest of Bengal.
The Kapoor family established the Burdwan Raj estate, a powerful zamindari owing revenue to the Mughal state.

politicalHistory.ruler: East India Company and Burdwan Raj
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The Company displaced the Nawab's political authority after Plassey; the Raj remained a major revenue estate under Company rule and the Permanent Settlement.
Burdwan was the headquarters of its Bengal division, while the Maharaja retained landed proprietary status under Crown paramountcy.
Burdwan Division remained in the reduced western province during the first partition.
The division continued under the reunited Bengal Province until independence.
Burdwan became part of India; the zamindari system was later abolished and the town remains a district centre in West Bengal.

name: Gour (Gauda)
historicalStatus: Ancient & Medieval Imperial Capital of Bengal
descriptionShort: Gour (Gauda) was the grand ruined imperial capital of ancient and medieval Bengal on the Malda border, famous for Boro Sona Masjid and Dakhil Darwaza.
descriptionLong: Capital of King Shashanka, Pala emperors, Sena kings, and independent Bengal Sultans (under Lakhnauti and Jannatabad), Gour was one of the greatest fortified cities in medieval Asia. Abandoned in the late 16th century due to an epidemic and river shift, its immense terracotta brick ruins remained legendary in 1905.
famousSpecialties: Medieval brick Sultanate architecture (Boro Sona Masjid, Dakhil Darwaza, Firoz Minar), ancient Buddhist-Hindu capital ruins, and Malda Fazli mangoes.
revolutionarySignificance: Historical symbol of sovereign medieval Bengali imperial pride invoked heavily by Swadeshi poets and nationalists during anti-partition rallies.

politicalHistory.periodDetails: Gour was the traditional capital of the Sena kingdom immediately before Bakhtiyar Khalji's conquest.

politicalHistory.ruler: Ghurid successor rulers and Delhi Sultanate
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Bakhtiyar Khalji made Gour/Lakhnauti his base; Delhi-appointed governors and competing chiefs ruled the city thereafter.
Gour was a principal capital under the Ilyas Shahi and Husain Shahi dynasties and a centre of sultanate administration.
Sher Shah's successors and the Karrani dynasty controlled Gour until the Afghan defeat at Rajmahal; the capital shifted toward Tanda as Gour declined.
The Mughals incorporated the ruins and surrounding Malda tract into Bengal Subah; river change and epidemics prevented Gour's recovery.
The Malda region entered Company revenue administration after the battles of Plassey and Buxar.
The archaeological site remained under British district administration and was recorded in gazetteers.
Gour's ruins fell on the Indian side of the 1947 boundary and are now protected heritage remains in Malda district.

name: Plassey
historicalStatus: Site of the Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757)
descriptionShort: Palashi (Plassey) on the Bhagirathi river was the site of the historic 1757 battle that established British colonial rule in Bengal.
descriptionLong: On 23 June 1757, Robert Clive's 3,000 East India Company troops defeated Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah's 50,000-strong army after Mir Jafar and Rai Durlabh held back their divisions. Lord Curzon visited Plassey in 1901 and commissioned the Lord Curzon Monument obelisk at the battlefield.
famousSpecialties: Battlefield memorial obelisk, mango groves of Palashi along the Bhagirathi river, and historic EIC encampment grounds.
revolutionarySignificance: Watershed site marking the loss of Indian independence in 1757; invoked by Swadeshi revolutionaries as the symbol of colonial subjugation to be avenged.

politicalHistory.periodDetails: Palashi lay in the Nadia-Murshidabad corridor, successively governed by Bengal's sultans and their local officers.

politicalHistory.ruler: Mughal Empire and Nawabs of Bengal
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The battlefield was within Mughal Bengal and later the Nawab's effective domain, administered through zamindars and military officers.

politicalHistory.ruler: East India Company and Mir Jafar's Nawabate
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The Company's victory at Plassey made it the power behind the Nawab's court and redirected Bengal's political order.
After the Diwani of 1765, the Company administered the Nadia-Murshidabad countryside as part of the Bengal Presidency.
Palashi remained a settlement in British district administration; the battlefield became a colonial monument site.
Palashi remained in India after Partition and is now a heritage site in Nadia district.

name: Buxar
historicalStatus: Site of the Battle of Buxar (22 October 1764)
descriptionShort: Historic river town on the Ganges in Shahabad district, location of the 1764 battle that won the imperial Diwani of Bengal for the EIC.
descriptionLong: On 22 October 1764, Major Hector Munro defeated the combined forces of Nawab Mir Qasim of Bengal, Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh, and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, solidifying total EIC mastery over Eastern India.
famousSpecialties: Historic Buxar Fort, Ramayana heritage sites (Rameshwar Nath Temple), and strategic Ganges river passage.
revolutionarySignificance: Site of the decisive 1764 battle that granted the British legal revenue rights (Diwani) over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.

politicalHistory.ruler: Delhi Sultanate, Bengal Sultanate and local chiefs
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Buxar lay on the frontier between Bihar and eastern India, under shifting Sultanate and regional authority.

politicalHistory.ruler: Mughal Empire and Nawabs of Bengal
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The Ganges town formed part of Mughal Bihar and later the Nawab's wider Bengal-Bihar sphere.
The Company defeated the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and Shah Alam II at Buxar on 22 October 1764.
The victory secured the 1765 Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and brought Buxar into Company revenue administration.
Buxar remained under Crown rule as a river town in the Bihar administrative system.
Buxar became part of India and is now administered as a district of Bihar.

name: Puri
historicalStatus: Sacred Pilgrimage City & District Headquarters
descriptionShort: Puri on the Bay of Bengal coast was world-famous for the 12th-century Jagannath Temple, annual Ratha Yatra festival, and coastal heritage.
descriptionLong: One of the Char Dham pilgrimage sites of India, Puri centers around the monumental Jagannath Temple built by King Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva. It was headquarters of Puri district in Orissa Division, spiritual seat of the Gajapati Maharaja of Puri.
famousSpecialties: 12th-century Jagannath Temple, annual Ratha Yatra (Chariot Festival), Mahaprasad culinary heritage, Khaja sweet, and Golden Beach.
revolutionarySignificance: Center of Oriya spiritual identity; site of Khurda Paika Rebellion (1817) led by Bakshi Jagabandhu against British revenue oppression.

politicalHistory.ruler: Eastern Ganga and Gajapati kings of Odisha
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Puri and the Jagannath temple were governed within the Ganga and Gajapati kingdom, with the temple under royal patronage.
Afghan and Mughal conquest placed coastal Odisha under northern imperial administrations while the Gajapati religious office continued.
Maratha rulers controlled Odisha and maintained the political-religious relationship with the Gajapati of Puri.
The Company occupied Odisha in 1803; Puri became a district headquarters while temple management remained a central local question.
Puri was administered in the Bengal Presidency through the Orissa Division under Crown rule.
Puri joined India in 1947 and remains the sacred pilgrimage capital of Odisha, with the temple's hereditary and state institutions continuing in modern form.

name: Cooch Behar
historicalStatus: Capital of the Princely State of Cooch Behar
descriptionShort: Capital of the feudatory Koch dynasty princely state, featuring Victor Jubilee Palace built by Maharaja Nripendra Narayan in 1887.
descriptionLong: Founded by Biswa Singha of the Koch dynasty in 1515, Cooch Behar remained an autonomous princely state in treaty alliance with the British Crown. Maharaja Nripendra Narayan modernized the city with European classical architecture.
famousSpecialties: Italian Renaissance style Victor Jubilee Palace (Cooch Behar Palace), Madan Mohan Temple, and Rajbari parklands.
revolutionarySignificance: Autonomous Koch dynastic capital under British supervisory treaty; key strategic gateway between North Bengal, Assam, and Bhutan.

politicalHistory.periodDetails: The northern frontier was governed by changing Kamarupa, Kamata and local polities before the rise of the Koch dynasty.
Biswa Singha consolidated the Koch kingdom and established Cooch Behar as its capital.
The Koch state retained internal rule while navigating Afghan and Mughal expansion in North Bengal and Assam.

politicalHistory.ruler: Koch Behar rulers under Mughal suzerainty
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Cooch Behar remained a distinct kingdom, acknowledging Mughal influence in the surrounding plains.

politicalHistory.ruler: Cooch Behar princely state under British paramountcy
politicalHistory.periodDetails: After conflict with Bhutan and British intervention, Cooch Behar became a protected princely state; the Maharaja retained internal authority.
The state continued briefly after Indian independence before the ruler signed the instrument of accession.
Cooch Behar was merged into India in 1950 and is now a district and historic city of West Bengal.

name: Agartala
historicalStatus: Capital of the Princely State of Hill Tippera (Tripura)
descriptionShort: Capital of the ancient Manikya dynasty of Hill Tippera state, home to Ujjayanta Palace built by Maharaja Radha Kishore Manikya.
descriptionLong: Moved from Old Agartala by Maharaja Krishna Manikya in 1760, Agartala was the royal seat of Maharaja Radha Kishore Manikya in 1905, who was a close friend and patron of Rabindranath Tagore.
famousSpecialties: Ujjayanta Palace architecture, Tripura Manikya royal heritage, bamboo and cane craft, and patronage of Bengali literature.
revolutionarySignificance: Independent Manikya kingdom sanctuary; royal patron Maharaja Radha Kishore Manikya funded Rabindranath Tagore's educational and Swadeshi efforts.

politicalHistory.periodDetails: The Manikya kingdom controlled the hill country and extended influence into the Tippera plains, balancing Bengal Sultanate pressure.

politicalHistory.ruler: Manikya dynasty and Bengal Sultanate/Mughal suzerainty
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Tripura remained a distinct kingdom while the plains were contested by Bengal's Afghan and Mughal authorities.
Krishna Manikya moved the royal seat to Agartala in 1760; the kingdom maintained internal sovereignty under growing British influence.

politicalHistory.ruler: Hill Tippera princely state under British paramountcy
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The Manikya Maharaja governed the protected state while British political officers supervised external affairs.
Agartala remained the capital of the autonomous princely state, adjacent to the new Eastern Bengal and Assam province.
The state acceded to India after independence and was administered under a Chief Commissioner.

politicalHistory.ruler: Republic of India: Union Territory of Tripura
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Tripura became a centrally administered territory after merger with India.

politicalHistory.ruler: Republic of India: State of Tripura
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Tripura attained full statehood in 1972; Agartala remains its capital.

name: Serampore
historicalStatus: Former Danish Settlement (1755–1845) & Serampore Mission Press
descriptionShort: Historic Hugli river town famous as Danish Frederiksnagore until 1845, site of William Carey's Serampore Mission Press.
descriptionLong: Leased to Denmark in 1755, Serampore became a sanctuary for Baptist missionaries William Carey, Joshua Marshman, and William Ward, who founded Serampore College (1818) and the first vernacular printing presses in India.
famousSpecialties: First Indian language metal type printing press (Serampore Trio), Serampore College (1818), Danish colonial architecture, and textile weaving.
revolutionarySignificance: Cradle of Bengal's vernacular printing revolution (Samachar Darpan - 1818); active in 1905 Swadeshi boycott meetings.

politicalHistory.periodDetails: The Hooghly river settlement lay within the western provinces of the Bengal Sultanate.
Mughal revenue and port authorities governed the area while European companies established river factories.
Denmark leased Serampore from the Nawab's government and maintained a sovereign trading settlement and mission centre.
Denmark ceded the settlement to Britain in 1845; it was incorporated into Hooghly district.
Serampore remained a municipality and river town under Crown district administration.
Serampore became part of India and remains a municipality in Hooghly district.

name: Chandernagore
historicalStatus: French Sovereign Enclave in Bengal
descriptionShort: Sovereign French enclave on the Hugli river inside Hooghly district, famous for French Strand promenade and revolutionary sanctuary.
descriptionLong: Established in 1673 by French Governor Joseph François Dupleix, Chandernagore remained under French sovereignty until 1950. It served as a vital sanctuary for freedom fighters like Sri Aurobindo and Rash Behari Bose during revolutionary underground operations.
famousSpecialties: French colonial architecture, Hugli riverfront Strand, Farashdanga fine muslin sarees, and Jagaddhatri Puja celebrations.
revolutionarySignificance: Sovereign French territory serving as a safe sanctuary for revolutionary leaders (Sri Aurobindo, Rash Behari Bose, Kanailal Dutta) to evade British police arrests.

politicalHistory.periodDetails: The riverbank settlement was successively within Bengal's Sultanate and Mughal administrative sphere.

politicalHistory.ruler: French East India Company under Mughal suzerainty
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The French established a trading settlement at Chandernagore while the Mughal authorities retained formal sovereignty.
British forces captured the French settlement during the Seven Years' War and held it during the struggle for Bengal.
Chandernagore was restored to France in 1763 and remained a sovereign enclave administered from Pondicherry, despite British dominance around it.
After Indian independence, a local referendum supported union with India; France transferred de facto control in 1950 and sovereignty in 1952.
Chandernagore became part of India and was incorporated into West Bengal in 1955.

name: Bishnupur
historicalStatus: Capital of Mallabhum Malla Kings & Terracotta Temple Center
descriptionShort: Historic capital of Malla kings in Bankura district, renowned for 17th-century terracotta Krishna temples and Bishnupuri classical music.
descriptionLong: Ruled by the Malla dynasty for over a thousand years, Bishnupur developed a distinct architectural style featuring laterite and terracotta temples (Rasmancha, Jor Bangla, Madan Mohan) built under King Veer Hambir.
famousSpecialties: 17th-century carved terracotta temples, Bishnupuri Swarnachari & Baluchari silk sarees, Bishnupur Classical Music Gharana, and Dalmadal cannon.
revolutionarySignificance: Historical capital of sovereign Mallabhum Hindu kingdom, celebrated by Swadeshi historians for resisting Mughal hegemony.

politicalHistory.periodDetails: Bishnupur was the fortified capital of the Malla kingdom, which maintained autonomy between Bengal powers and Odisha.
The Mallas retained internal rule while paying tribute and recognizing the authority of the Mughal Bengal Subah.

politicalHistory.ruler: East India Company and Bishnupur Raj
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Company revenue authority followed the Diwani; the Malla estate survived as a zamindari under the Permanent Settlement.
Bishnupur was administered within Bankura district while its former royal family retained landed privileges.
Bankura and Bishnupur remained in western Bengal during the partition of the province.
The town continued within Bengal's Bankura district until independence.
Bishnupur became part of India; the zamindari order was abolished and the former capital is now a protected heritage town.

name: Tamluk
historicalStatus: Ancient International Seaport of Tamralipta
descriptionShort: Sub-divisional town in Midnapore district, identified as ancient maritime port of Tamralipta visited by Xuanzang and Faxian.
descriptionLong: Mentioned in the Mahabharata and Greco-Roman records (Ptolemy), Tamralipta was the primary sea gateway from northern India to Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, and China during the Mauryan and Gupta eras.
famousSpecialties: Ancient Tamralipta archaeological artifacts, Bargabhima Temple (Shakti Peetha), and Rupnarayan river estuary commerce.
revolutionarySignificance: Historic center of Midnapore anti-colonial resistance; later site of the famous Tamralipta Jatiya Sarkar parallel government in 1942.

politicalHistory.ruler: Local chiefs, Bengal Sultanate and Gajapati Odisha
politicalHistory.periodDetails: The former Tamralipta zone lay at the meeting point of Bengal's southwestern frontier and Odisha's northern coastal sphere.
Mughal conquest of Odisha brought the Tamluk area into the imperial Orissa administration, mediated by local zamindars.
Maratha control of Odisha and its northern approaches shaped the political setting of Tamluk.
The Company occupied Odisha in 1803; Tamluk remained a sub-divisional centre in Midnapore district.
Tamluk was administered through Midnapore district; its older port had become a riverine and agrarian centre.
Tamluk joined India and remains the headquarters of Purba Medinipur district in West Bengal.

name: Sonargaon
historicalStatus: Ancient Capital of East Bengal & Bengal Sultanate Seat
descriptionShort: Historic capital of Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah and Isa Khan (Baro-Bhuyan leader), famous for Panam City merchant mansions.
descriptionLong: Capital of eastern Bengal from the 13th to 17th centuries, Sonargaon was described by Ibn Battuta and Ralph Fitch as a flourishing metropolis famed for gold trade and woven cloth.
famousSpecialties: Panam City (Painam Nagar) architectural merchant mansions, Folk Art & Crafts Museum, and Bengal Sultanate royal tombs.
revolutionarySignificance: Capital of Isa Khan and the Baro-Bhuyans (Twelve Chieftains) who fiercely resisted Akbar's Mughal expansion into East Bengal.

politicalHistory.ruler: Sena successor rulers and Deva dynasty
politicalHistory.periodDetails: After the fall of Sena power in western Bengal, the Deva rulers retained authority in eastern Bengal; Sonargaon emerged as a capital in the Vanga region under Danuja Rai.
The independent Hindu polity in eastern Bengal was absorbed into the expanding Muslim provincial system, with Sonargaon retaining regional importance.
Muhammad bin Tughluq reorganized Bengal into Lakhnauti, Satgaon and Sonargaon; Sonargaon became the headquarters of the eastern province.
Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah established an independent sultanate at Sonargaon, followed by his son Ikhtiyaruddin Ghazi Shah, before Ilyas Shah unified Bengal.
After Ilyas Shah's conquest, Sonargaon became a provincial metropolis within the unified Bengal Sultanate while remaining a major port and commercial centre.
The authority of the Ilyas Shahi line was interrupted by Raja Ganesha and his successors; Sonargaon remained one of eastern Bengal's principal political centres.

politicalHistory.ruler: Restored Ilyas Shahi and Husain Shahi sultans
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Restored Ilyas Shahi rulers and then the Husain Shahi dynasty governed Sonargaon through provincial officials; its muslin and overseas trade remained prominent.
The independent sultanate fell to Afghan power after 1538; Sonargaon remained an important eastern centre during the Sur and Karrani periods.

politicalHistory.ruler: Mughal Empire contested by the Baro-Bhuyans
politicalHistory.periodDetails: Mughal claims followed the conquest of Bengal, but Isa Khan and Musa Khan made Sonargaon the centre of resistance in the Bhati riverlands until Islam Khan's campaigns.
After Musa Khan's submission, Sonargaon became a Mughal sarkar headquarters; the transfer of the provincial capital to Dhaka accelerated its political decline.
The surrounding Dacca district passed into Company influence after Plassey and the Diwani; Sonargaon declined while Panam became a nineteenth-century merchant settlement.
Sonargaon was administered within Dacca district under Crown rule and survived chiefly as a rural and commercial locality with important historic remains.
Partition placed Sonargaon in the eastern province of Pakistan, initially named East Bengal.
The province was renamed East Pakistan in 1955; Sonargaon remained within Dacca district until the Liberation War.
Following Bangladesh's independence, Sonargaon became part of Narayanganj District and is now protected and interpreted as a major archaeological and cultural heritage area.
